items.extracted_title: Kazakhstan Expands Compute for Its AI Future
items.extracted_excerpt: The nation is scaling its compute foundation through planned NVIDIA Vera Rubin infrastructure deployments, with AI-native companies fueling the next phase of growth.
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: Kazakhstan’s AI ecosystem is moving from infrastructure plans to deployment. The shift is visible across the full AI stack — from infrastructure to models to applications. The announcements below — coinciding with a visit to Astana by NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang — point to the nation’s increasing supply of accelerated computing, along with its growing demand for what comes next. On Friday, Oct. 23, NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang visited Astana, meeting with President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev at the Akorda Presidential Palace and joining Deputy Prime Minister Zhaslan Madiyev — Kazakhstan’s minister of AI and digital development — for a public fireside chat at the Alem.AI program. Jensen Huang and Kazakhstan’s AI Minister Speak at Alem.AI In their fireside chat at Alem.AI, Kazakhstan’s international center for artificial intelligence, Madiyev and Huang discussed the country’s push to become an AI nation — building the energy and computing infrastructure to support homegrown AI and applying it across the economy. Madiyev said Kazakhstan wants AI that reflects its language and culture. “We want AI that understands and speaks Kazakh and captures cultural contexts and cultural specifics,” he said, describing the country’s work on Kazakh-language models. Huang said Kazakhstan could turn its energy resources into a foundation for AI production — and a new kind of export. “Instead of just exporting energy, in the future, you could transform energy into intelligence and export intelligence,” he said. He also argued that local data is central to that ambition: it embodies a country’s culture, history and values. “Your country’s data is your natural resource. It belongs to you.” The conversation also turned to physical AI. Madiyev pointed to Kazakhstan’s factories, mines, agriculture, transport and logistics as potential areas for development, asking how the country could become a hub for training models for robots and other physical systems. Huang called the idea “fantastic,” saying physical AI could transform industries from mining and mineral processing to agriculture. Huang said AI and robotics can help people do more, but ambition will shape how fully they seize that opportunity. He applied the idea to Kazakhstan, saying AI could help lift the country and its people. “If you have ambition, and I believe you do, AI will lift your nation,” Huang said. “AI will lift your people.” Huang also praised the founders of Higgsfield AI, the Kazakhstan-founded startup, and it was announced NVIDIA is making an investment into the startup during the event. “The first thing and the last thing is you invest in people, not companies,” he said, describing the founders as visionary and pointing to their effort to compete globally. Asked about AI security, Huang said the technology must be developed and deployed responsibly. He described NVIDIA’s OpenShell as a way to contain AI agents by limiting their access to files and tools and monitoring their activity. For young people entering a fast-changing field, Huang recommended learning how AI works — not just how to use it. He said aspiring AI programmers should understand the technology’s principles, strengths and weaknesses, combining technical knowledge with the ability to work effectively with AI. “I envy being 18 years old today… because the world is changing so rapidly, and there’s a complete reset because of technology.” The Infrastructure Layer Is Scaling The visits coincided with a signing ceremony marking Firebird’s investment agreement with the government of Kazakhstan, held at the presidential palace. Building on its first AI factory in Armenia, Firebird is expanding into Kazakhstan, where it has secured a U.S. export license for 45,000 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs. The first phase is under construction with Kazakhtelecom at Data Center Valley, targeting commercial launch in the third quarter of 2027. A planned second phase would bring Firebird’s total potential AI infrastructure capacity in Kazakhstan to approximately 500 megawatts. Firebird also plans to establish Firebird Labs Kazakhstan to support local AI startups, research and talent development through funding, access to compute and research partnerships. Firebird cofounder and CEO Razmig Hovaghimian attended the signing ceremony at the Akorda Presidential Palace alongside government officials. “What began as a seed of an idea 180 days ago has grown into a major investment in Kazakhstan’s AI future,” said Razmig Hovaghimian, co-Founder and CEO of Firebird. “President Tokayev’s vision gave us the confidence to think bigger about what we can build together. With Jensen Huang here today, that ambition feels more tangible than ever. We’re building the infrastructure for Kazakhstan’s talent and ideas to reach the world.” Kazakhtelecom, the nation’s largest telecommunications company, has already deployed 400 NVIDIA H200 and 480 NVIDIA B300 GPUs in Astana and Almaty. Next year, the company plans to deploy more than 1,000 GPUs in the Data Center Valley, along with more than 1,000 NVIDIA Vera Rubin GPUs in the Ekibastuz region, serving diverse workloads with infrastructure that enterprises, developers and institutions can use at scale. An Honorary Black Belt for Huang Later that day, also at the Akorda Presidential Palace, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev presented Huang with an honorary black belt in Judo. The belt, embroidered in gold stitching, was a special thanks from President Tokayev for Huang’s support of Kazakhstan’s AI ambition and for leadership aligned with the spirit and rigor of the martial art. At the end of their meeting President Tokayev had another honor for Huang, presenting him with the Order of Dostyk, First Class, for Huang’s contribution to the development of artificial intelligence in Kazakhstan. Dostyk means friendship and the Order honors peace, friendship and cooperation. AI-Native Companies Scale With Compute And that development is accelerating. The nation’s AI-native companies are also building out their compute capacity — and the applications that run atop them. Higgsfield is expanding its AI infrastructure with NVIDIA Vera Rubin running on cloud service providers, giving the company additional capacity as models, products and customer demand for its generative media applications grow. inDrive and Pony.ai are also collaborating to explore robotaxi services in Kazakhstan, with Astana as the first deployment city. The companies will assess the feasibility of bringing Pony.ai’s seventh-generation robotaxis to the inDrive app, supported by NVIDIA AI infrastructure, built on the NVIDIA Hyperion sensor and compute platform with the NVIDIA Halos safety system. More local capacity gives developers and companies room to train, fine-tune and serve increasingly capable models. Successful applications, in turn, create demand for more compute. items.extracted_title: Rapidly scaling online storage to serve over 1 billion ChatGPT users (Part II)
items.extracted_excerpt: Learn how OpenAI scaled Habitat with reliable multi-tenancy, global caching, and Azure Cosmos DB to deliver 12× faster reads for ChatGPT.
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: All OpenAI products require fast, reliable access to data, provided by our storage platform, Habitat. It has to respond in milliseconds to over 1 billion users across 40 geographic regions. Our infrastructure faced an extraordinary challenge: supporting explosive growth and new use cases while continuing to improve reliability, performance, and product developer velocity. Solving that challenge required rethinking how our online storage platform was designed and operated. We constantly evaluated tradeoffs, following the pattern of: first become reliable enough for mission-critical product traffic, then fast enough for global users, and, finally, to deftly operate at massive scale. This two-part series explains how we developed Habitat from a simple client library and database into a globally distributed storage platform serving over 500 petabytes of data. Part I focused on Habitat’s evolution from a Python client to a service. It also covered the techniques that allowed us to push a Python-based service far beyond what many would consider practical. In this post, Part II, we walk through how we scaled the underlying storage component: Azure Cosmos DB. Through a close working partnership with the Azure team, we arrived at a viable multi-tenancy approach of co-managed containers, with excellent read performance at massive, global scale. As companies scale, infra teams often evolve from running single-tenant systems to multi-tenant ones. Single-tenancy, where every product surface team maintains their own system, reduces blast radius and provides easy ownership boundaries and workload isolation. As teams and product surfaces grow, this becomes expensive to run. Single-tenancy makes every product team responsible for capacity planning and often results in significant over-provisioning. Conversely, multi-tenancy assigns control to a centralized database team, with better knowledge and experience for provisioning resources. But multi-tenancy creates its own problems, such as noisy-neighbor issues, where one tenant consumes an unusually large share of the resources to the detriment of the other tenants. In Habitat, we had to weigh all these tradeoffs to design a reliable, efficient, storage system at scale. Today, Habitat is a multi-tenant database layer for many OpenAI products, but we went through a circular journey from using one multi-tenant Azure Cosmos DB container to provisioning single-tenant backing containers to reverting to a multi-tenant container by default. We’re still very early in our multi-tenancy story on Habitat: we support a large set of use cases, but we’ve been able to defer investment in this area by leveraging Azure Cosmos DB’s built-in primitives wherever possible. Before walking through our Azure Cosmos DB journey, some basic context: - An Azure Cosmos DB account defines a set of containers and a replication policy - Each container is provisioned for a certain amount of throughput in request units per second (RU/s) - Data within each container is stored in a typical shard-by-specified-logical-partition-key manner with documented limits on storage and throughput per logical partition key - Azure Cosmos DB handles sharding logical partition keys across fewer backing physical partitions, splitting them into multiple physical partitions when storage exceeds a threshold or when the container requires more physical partitions to sustain the provisioned throughput We originally allowed any client load through, relying on the stated 10K RU/s limit per logical partition key to provide back pressure. When we first set out, we also used only one default Azure Cosmos DB container in each account. This worked well enough, but proved problematic for a few reasons: Due to early API choices, we exposed logical partition key selection directly to clients. As a result, we have frequent collisions on commonly used partition keys, such as user_id or workspace_id, across different product use cases. Because these use cases shared Azure Cosmos DB limits on the same logical partition keys, the design constrained overall throughput for a given user. One common problem we faced in scaling Postgres before we moved to Habitat and Azure Cosmos DB was the ability for many requests from a very hot organization or hot key—one tenant generating a disproportionately high load—to take out the whole database. Significant collective effort was spent to cache those keys and build leases into cache misses so that the resulting cache miss load does not stomp on the underlying database. While documented data size and throughput limits apply to logical partition keys, the physical partition is actually where limits are enforced. In practice, this means logical partitions are unable to reach 10,000 RU/s. Instead, they share the physical partition’s limits with every other logical partition key colocated on that physical partition. This allowed noisy neighbors to impact many unrelated logical partition keys, with workloads operating on data for niche product features disrupting core login and signup flows. The throughput limit for a given physical partition is also variable, dependent on the total throughput assigned to the Azure Cosmos DB container. The container’s provisioned throughput is distributed roughly evenly across the physical partitions for that container. As data volume grows, physical partitions split, increasing the total partition count while total provisioned throughput remains unchanged. The result is that the effective throughput limit per partition shrinks as data size grows. For our most storage-heavy, blob-like use cases, this creates a failure mode where storage growth alone reduces throughput capacity for active workloads even while request rates and usage remain stable. Separate containers help partially solve these partition key limits and noisy neighbors. By using separate containers, each can be assigned its own independent physical partitions and only the varying workloads on that container itself could be noisy neighbors or overlap in partition key space. On the downside, there is non-zero overhead in provisioning new containers—each container requires individualized capacity planning—so we want to create containers only at a service or use case boundary that makes sense. We began to use separate Azure Cosmos DB containers for the most critical new use cases requiring strong isolation. Combined with a script for managing weak partitions by synchronizing the total throughput provisioned for each container with its number of physical partitions, we mostly avoided all the problems we were facing. However, since we started with a default container, many legacy critical use cases were unfortunately stuck there without a data migration. To protect critical services that still relied on data in the shared default container, we often advised teams to create separate containers for new services or major product features. items.summary_en: OpenAI explains how we strengthened containment for frontier model training and evaluation, including offline environments and high-compute red-teaming.
items.extracted_title: Securing our frontier model training environment
items.extracted_excerpt: OpenAI explains how we strengthened containment for frontier model training and evaluation, including offline environments and high-compute red-teaming.
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: Securing our frontier model training environment We’ve strengthened containment for internal frontier-model training and evaluation and used our strongest models to red-team the boundaries. This post describes how we secure the environments that we use to train and evaluate frontier models. These research settings differ from those in which customers use our released models: models in development may not yet have completed safety and alignment training, and we deliberately test them under adversarial conditions to expose weaknesses. Before making models available for broader use, we conduct safety and alignment assessments and put production safeguards in place. In order to work with software, AI models need computing environments: digital workspaces where they can write and run code, search for information, and attempt different approaches to solving problems. These environments allow models to practice these skills, while also restricting what they can access or do—helping contain the consequences when models make mistakes or exhibit misaligned behavior. But as models become more capable, they become better at finding ways around those limits. A sophisticated model might exploit a software flaw or misconfiguration to escape a sandbox, exploit an internal service to reach the live internet, or find unauthorized ways to communicate with agents in other sandboxes. The Hugging Face incident in July, as well as other examples of model misalignment(opens in a new window) that we’ve observed, demonstrates how models with sophisticated cyber capabilities can bypass containment during their training and evaluation. In response to those incidents, we’ve substantially hardened the security of our research environments. Working closely with cloud providers, we’ve added new controls throughout our infrastructure, reduced the attack surface that agents can exploit, and improved our methods for detecting misaligned behavior and attempts to cross security boundaries. These protections overlap, so that containment can hold even if an individual control fails—a strategy known as defense in depth. Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access. We’ve implemented this policy and will maintain it until advances in these safeguards justify broader internet access. These investments have allowed us to detect and stop sophisticated misaligned behavior before it causes damage. On September 20, for example, an internal research model exploited a misconfiguration in a DNS resolver to gain limited access to the live internet during a training run(opens in a new window). Although we contained the incident, it exposed weaknesses that required further work. We paused training and evaluation of our most capable models and used that pause to further harden our infrastructure, strengthen our monitoring, and improve the systems that automatically stop runs when we detect activity that poses a serious risk. But increasingly capable models can find vulnerabilities or misconfigurations in even the most secure systems. To ensure the resilience of our research environments against even the most powerful models, we launched a high-compute red-teaming campaign to probe weaknesses in our infrastructure. Teams of frontier-model agents were tasked with finding vulnerabilities and misconfigurations that could allow them to take unauthorized actions—like accessing the live internet, escaping security boundaries, or conducting unauthorized communication with other agents. These red-teaming experiments discovered previously unknown software vulnerabilities, as well as misconfigurations in our research infrastructure. We’ve remediated weaknesses our red-teaming agents discovered and—where these issues were present in open-source software—have worked with the relevant maintainers, under our Patch the Planet initiative, to disclose and fix them. As our red-teaming experiments continued, the number of vulnerabilities and misconfigurations that our agents identified declined significantly. While we view this as an encouraging signal about the strength of our infrastructure, we expect that future models will be able to identify and exploit vulnerabilities of which we’re not yet aware. We therefore view continuous red-teaming as a core part of our long-term strategy for strengthening the security of our research environments. Accordingly, we’ve made high-compute red-teaming part of the safety cases we use to evaluate whether our frontier training and evaluation runs can proceed securely. With our assessments completed and enhanced controls put in place, we resumed reinforcement learning (RL) training and internal inference of our frontier models on October 1. In this post, we discuss how we’ve strengthened the environments we use to train and evaluate our models, and how we use our most powerful models to find and repair weaknesses in our systems. Our approach to containment starts with a paramount requirement: the limits on what an agent can access must hold even when the agent tries to circumvent them. We define a strict security boundary around the resources the agent is authorized to use and design the surrounding infrastructure to enforce that boundary—even when agents make sustained, sophisticated attempts to breach it. Inside the security boundary, agents can have access to browsers, code execution environments, computer-use tools, and other services they might need for their tasks. Agents that are explicitly authorized to communicate can also share particular resources within the same boundary. Everything else—everything that the agent is not explicitly authorized to access—must remain out of reach. If agents can access the infrastructure that hosts them, communicate with agents outside permitted channels, or reach external systems, that constitutes a failure of containment. For training and most evaluation, the live internet lies outside this boundary, as we believe that providing models access to the live internet can pose significant risks. Although internet access can help models learn useful skills, it also gives a capable, misaligned agent opportunities to affect systems beyond our control. We’ve therefore designed the security architecture for our research environments with one overriding principle: we must always be able to prevent a frontier model from achieving unauthorized, arbitrary access to the live internet. While we want to prevent models from gaining arbitrary access to the live internet, it’s also important that they learn how to browse, search for information, and work with web applications. items.extracted_excerpt: OpenAI and Poland’s NASK are partnering on AI safety, security, and technical research to strengthen safeguards and support a more resilient digital ecosystem.
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: OpenAI and Poland’s NASK National Research Institute have signed an agreement to explore collaboration on AI safety, security and technical research. The partnership will bring together expertise from both organizations to better understand emerging risks, strengthen safeguards, and explore how advanced AI can contribute to a more secure and resilient digital ecosystem. As AI systems become more capable, international collaboration between developers and public research institutions will be essential to understanding their risks and building stronger safeguards. OpenAI’s existing work with the US Center for Advancing Standards and Innovation for Super Intelligence (CAISSI), UK AI Security Institute (AISI) and other public research institutions around the world has already helped strengthen safeguards, identify and fix security vulnerabilities in AI agents, and advance frontier AI safety. Through the agreement, NASK’s AI Safety Research Center – serving as the Polish Artificial Intelligence Safety Institute (AISI) – and OpenAI will collaborate on AI safety research, exploring ways to evaluate increasingly capable AI systems, identify potential vulnerabilities and strengthen safeguards. OpenAI has called for the US to work with countries around the world on international technical standards for frontier AI, drawing on the expertise of AI safety institutes and standards bodies. Common approaches to evaluating capabilities, assessing risks, testing safeguards and reporting incidents can help countries compare evidence and respond to risks that cross borders. The collaboration with NASK reflects the value of bringing national expertise into this wider effort. In NASK’s case, this expertise rests on extensive research in AI safety, applied directly to protecting public services and Poland’s digital information ecosystem. Without national partners like NASK, global AI safety standards may remain detached from the realities in which AI is actually used. The agreement also builds on OpenAI’s existing work with cyber defenders in Poland. In July, CERT Polska, which operates within NASK, gained access(opens in a new window) to OpenAI’s cyber capable models through Daybreak. The team used OpenAI models to help discover six vulnerabilities in MikroTik RouterOS, including flaws that could be combined to take control of affected devices without authentication. The vendor released fixes, which CERT Polska confirmed prevented the attacks it observed.

items.extracted_title: LitPivot: Developing research ideas through dynamic contextualization within the literature landscape
items.extracted_excerpt: A Blog post by Ai2 on Hugging Face
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: LitPivot: Developing research ideas through dynamic contextualization within the literature landscape 📄 Paper Encountering a new paper can change a research idea's trajectory. The researcher may discover that someone has already addressed their proposed contribution, or find an unresolved problem in the paper that inspires a new direction of inquiry. We call this process a literature-initiated pivot: a change in research direction prompted by reading prior work. It connects two activities that researchers often have to manage separately: developing an idea and deciding which literature to measure it against. With collaborators at the University of Pennsylvania, we developed LitPivot, a system that helps researchers navigate these pivots. Using papers retrieved through Asta Paper Finder, LitPivot organizes literature around the part of a proposal being edited, offers critiques supported by excerpts from selected studies, and suggests revisions that researchers can accept, edit, or reject. LitPivot is intended to be used for early-stage research ideation, but the idea could possibly extend to longer writing tasks (i.e., writing the introduction section of a paper). In a study with 17 researchers, domain experts rated research ideas developed with LitPivot as better grounded in the literature than those developed with a text editor and an AI chat tool. Participants also perceived their revised research ideas as more novel and useful, and reported a stronger understanding of the surrounding literature. LitPivot will be presented at UIST 2026 in Detroit. Read the paper here. Research ideas evolve through engaging with the literature. In our analysis of meeting notes from four completed computer science research projects, we identified 21 literature-initiated pivots across all four projects. These fell into two types: differentiating an idea from existing work to establish an idea’s novelty, and aligning an idea with existing work to build on it. This project itself went through two pivots before we settled on its contributions. These changes can be difficult to navigate. In a formative study, five researchers developed proposals using a text editor and standard search tools. They struggled to develop their ideas while critically evaluating them against the literature. When a paper challenged an idea’s novelty, they wanted concrete suggestions for how to revise it, supported by prior work. These findings shaped LitPivot’s assessments, which pair literature-supported critiques with specific suggestions for revising the selected part of an idea. In LitPivot, a researcher starts by writing a short proposal in an editor and enabling what we call facet highlighting, which segments an articulated idea into different facets (i.e., a problem, contribution, and evaluation). To check a proposed facet, the researcher clicks that segment in the draft. An adjacent panel groups related papers based on the selected facet (e.g., grouping papers by the evaluation methods they use when the evaluation facet is selected) and highlights the most relevant groups. The researcher selects papers, requests an assessment, and reviews a suggested revision alongside excerpts supporting the critique. The literature is then reranked based on relevance to the revised facet. In particular, LitPivot separates a research idea into its problem, proposed contribution, and evaluation plan. Each facet has its own set and relevance ranking of related literature. LitPivot groups retrieved papers around the facet being edited, letting the researcher choose which ones the system should use to assess the draft. Alongside scientific-writing environments such as Prism and agentic assistants such as Claude Code, LitPivot explores a new workflow for developing an early research idea: choosing literature to assess it against, using that evidence to revise it, and reconsidering which papers matter as the idea changes. Its paper groups and linked critiques make those steps explicit for each part of the proposal, while researchers control both the draft and the evidence used to assess it. For a problem statement, LitPivot looks for evidence that the problem exists and reasons it matters. To assess a proposed contribution, it compares what the selected papers have already addressed with the limitations and future work they describe, looking for remaining gaps. For an evaluation plan, it checks whether the proposed tests address the research question and how similar work has been evaluated. The system then suggests a rewrite with supporting quotes attached. Changing one facet of an idea can leave another out of date. LitPivot flags passages that may need revision, such as an evaluation plan that no longer adequately evaluates a revised contribution. Researchers can accept, edit, or reject suggestions, and request new papers or refresh the literature ranking as their proposal develops. Paraphrased example from one study participant. In our lab study, 17 researchers each developed one assigned idea with LitPivot and another with a baseline tool—a text editor and an AI tool for asking questions about selected papers. Both conditions used the same collection of papers. Two domain experts, unaware of which system had been used, rated the resulting proposals on a single criterion: how well they used relevant literature to support and justify the idea. Proposals developed with LitPivot received higher ratings. Participants in the same study also reported a stronger understanding of the surrounding literature and greater self-reported improvements in their ideas’ novelty and usefulness with LitPivot than with the baseline. Domain experts also reviewed the participants’ ideas and rated the ideas revised using LitPivot to be significantly better grounded in relevant literature. One participant in our lab study started with a proposal to generate consistent, factual synthetic medical notes. LitPivot identified consistency across multiple hospital visits as a potential gap in the selected literature. The participant reviewed abstracts and removed papers about single-visit notes. After another assessment, they narrowed the proposal to detecting contradictions across notes from multiple visits. The example shows how revising an idea and choosing the literature used to assess it can inform each other. In a follow-up study, five researchers used LitPivot on their own ongoing projects during 30-minute sessions. Participants used LitPivot across multiple project phases, not just at the beginning. Two used it to vet new ideas against the literature, while three used it to refine the framing of more mature ideas. One researcher highlighted how seeing parallel concepts from different domains helped them reframe their contribution. These studies suggest that LitPivot can support both early exploration and the refinement of an existing research direction. items.extracted_title: Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up
items.extracted_excerpt: We’re on a journey to advance and democratize artificial intelligence through open source and open science.
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: In a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do? The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself. The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory. To look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx-cc) and of Transformers to look at. At the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We plan to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks. Select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement: it loads the model with from_pretrained, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron"). On a Trainium2 (trn2) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container, install the packages, then run: python3 run.py No need for torchrun: the script launches its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded. A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version: hf buckets sync hf://buckets/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-neff-cache/neuronxcc- /tmp/neff_cache Each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel plan use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English. At the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS says nothing about throughput, or about longer generations. Everything the Space shows comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions. Each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly: import pandas as pd df = pd.read_parquet("hf://datasets/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support/data") df[df.model_id == "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B"][["neuronx_cc", "library", "library_version", "neuron_cores", "result"]] The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result. Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.
